name: Graph exploration by a single agent

origin.note: Shannon's maze-solving mouse Theseus (first prototype 1950) explored a $5\times5$ grid with constant memory per cell [Disser2019Pebbles]; the first impossibility theorem for finite automata is Budach's [Budach1978Labyrinths].

summary: One agent starts at a node of an unknown anonymous graph and must visit every node; how much memory does it need, which pebbles or knowledge make it possible, and how fast can it be?

primer.intro: Imagine a small cleaning machine put down in a large building with no map, where every room looks the same. We model the building as a **graph**: rooms are **nodes** and corridors are **edges** (each edge joins two nodes), and the machine is an **agent** that walks from node to node along edges; one crossing of one edge is a **move**. $n$ is the number of nodes and $m$ the number of edges; the **degree** of a node is the number of edges at it, and $\Delta$ is the largest degree. At each node the edges are numbered $0, 1, \dots$; these numbers are called **ports**, and the numbering at one node has nothing to do with the numbering at the next. The agent sees only the degree of its current node and the port by which it came in; nodes are **anonymous** (they have no names), so it cannot tell a node it has seen before from a new one. In the basic version (**perpetual exploration**) it must eventually visit every node of every connected graph, without ever having to stop, and the question is how few bits of **memory** (what the agent keeps from one move to the next) make this possible.

ideas.title: Leave by the next port (trees)
ideas.idea:
This is the algorithm Choose-Next of [Diks2004Tree], for graphs without cycles (trees); here the ports of a node of degree $d$ are numbered $1, \dots, d$.
1. Leave the **start node** (the node where you are placed) by port 1.
2. When you enter a node of degree $d$ by port $i$, leave it by port $(i \bmod d) + 1$, the next port in cyclic order (at a node of degree 1 this sends you straight back).
3. Repeat forever.
ideas.analysis: On a tree this is the rule "keep your right hand on the wall": the agent walks around the tree, and every edge is walked once in each direction before the walk repeats, so all $n$ nodes are visited within $2(n-1)$ moves. The agent only has to remember one port number, which [Diks2004Tree] count as $O(\log\Delta)$ bits, and they show that $\Omega(\log\Delta)$ bits are needed on trees, so this is optimal. On graphs with cycles the same rule can go round a cycle forever and miss nodes; there the right amount of memory is $\Theta(D\log\Delta)$ bits, with $D$ the diameter (the largest distance between two nodes) [Fraigniaud2005Automaton].
ideas.why_it_matters: Choosing the next port from the entry port alone is the basic move of almost every memory-efficient exploration algorithm, and the universal exploration sequences used for general graphs are a generalisation of it.

ideas.title: No stopping on a ring without a pebble
ideas.idea: Ask for more: the agent must visit every node **and then stop**, without knowing $n$ and without a **pebble** (an object it could drop on a node to recognise that node later). Take rings (cycles) of every size, numbered so that at every node port 0 leads clockwise and port 1 counterclockwise. In such a ring every node has degree 2 and every arrival looks the same, so what the agent sees never depends on the size of the ring. A deterministic agent (one with no random choices) therefore makes the same sequence of moves in every such ring. Since it explores and stops in, say, the ring of 3 nodes, it stops after some fixed number $T$ of moves, and it does the same in the ring of $T+2$ nodes.
ideas.analysis: In $T$ moves the agent can visit at most $T+1$ different nodes, so in the ring of $T+2$ nodes at least one node is never visited: the agent stopped too early. Extra memory does not help, because the problem is not remembering but recognising: the agent can never tell "I am back where I started" from "this is a new node that looks the same". This is why every stopping variant in the catalogue adds a pebble or knowledge of a bound $N \ge n$ [Dieudonne2012Tokens].
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that the hard part of exploration is often knowing when you are done, a theme that returns in dispersion, rendezvous and gathering.

ideas.title: Random walk
ideas.idea:
Allow the agent to flip coins, and tell it a number $N \ge n$.
1. At each node, pick one of the ports uniformly at random and take its edge.
2. Count the moves; stop after $2N^3$ moves.
ideas.analysis: [Aleliunas1979Random] proved that a random walk visits every node of a connected graph within $2m(n-1)$ moves on average. Since $m \le N^2/2$ and $n - 1 < N$, this average is below $N^3$; a walk that runs twice as long as its average cover time fails to cover the graph with probability at most $1/2$ (Markov's inequality), and repeating the walk lowers the failure probability further. The agent needs only a counter, $O(\log N)$ bits. A deterministic agent with the same memory also exists, but its algorithm (Reingold's log-space construction) is much harder [Reingold2008Undirected].
ideas.why_it_matters: The random-walk bound was the starting point for universal traversal and exploration sequences, which turn the random walk into a fixed list of port choices that works on every graph.

glossary.definition: the connected graph $G = (V, E)$ to be explored, with $n$ nodes, $m$ edges, maximum degree $\Delta$ and diameter $D$
an element of $E$, joining two nodes
the single mobile entity that walks along edges and computes; deterministic unless a variant says otherwise
nodes carry no names the agent can read
the local number of an edge at a node $v$ ($0, \dots, \deg(v)-1$ or $1, \dots, \deg(v)$ as each text says); the two ends of an edge may carry different numbers
$\deg(v)$, the number of edges at node $v$; $\Delta$ is the maximum degree
one traversal of one edge by the agent; time is the number of moves
the number of bits of the agent's state, kept from one move to the next
an object the agent carries and can drop on a node and pick up again
every node is eventually visited; the agent need not stop
every node is visited and the agent then stops, at any node
every node is visited and the agent then stops at its start node $s$
the node $s$ where the agent is placed

history:
Exploration began as **maze search by finite automata**. The first question was whether a machine with bounded memory can visit every node at all: Budach showed it cannot for mazes [Budach1978Labyrinths], Blum and Kozen showed that two pebbles or two automata are enough in mazes [Blum1978Compass], and Rollik showed that every finite team has a planar trap [Rollik1980Planar].

From there the community turned to **how much memory** an agent needs as a function of the graph: $\Theta(D\log\Delta)$ bits in general [Fraigniaud2005Automaton], $O(\log n)$ once $n$ is known [Reingold2008Undirected], and the effect of the termination requirement on trees [Diks2004Tree] [Ambuhl2011Tree]. Markers came next: what one pebble buys [Fraigniaud2006Reduced], and the exact exchange rate between pebbles and memory [Disser2019Pebbles]. Time was a secondary measure throughout.

measures.name: Time
measures.description: edge traversals until every node is visited (for periodic exploration: the period)

measures.name: Memory
measures.description: bits of agent memory; pebbles, if any, are counted separately

axes.name: Knowledge

values.label: nothing known about the graph
values.definition: The agent knows nothing about $G$: not $n$, $m$, $\Delta$ or $D$.

values.label: an upper bound on $n$ is known
values.definition: The agent is given an integer $N\ge n$ (an upper bound on the number of nodes) as input.

values.label: a complete map is known (for a dynamic graph: the whole schedule)
values.description: The offline setting: the walk can be planned in advance.
values.definition: The agent is given a graph isomorphic to $G$, with port numbers, and (where stated) its own position on it; for a dynamic graph, the whole sequence $(G_t)$.

axes.origin: Knowing the size of the graph is the classical way to let an exploring walk end. Aleliunas, Karp, Lipton, Lovász and Rackoff proved that a random walk on a connected graph visits every node within $2m(n-1)$ expected steps from any start (Theorem 4), so by Markov's inequality $O(mn\log n)\subseteq O(n^3\log n)$ steps cover it with high probability, and a step counter and the value of $n$ give a randomized explorer that stops [Aleliunas1979Random]; Reingold's log-space universal exploration sequences do the same deterministically when $n$ is known [Reingold2008Undirected] (Corollary 5.5). Without a bound and without a marker an agent cannot tell a cycle from a longer one, so it can explore perpetually but never stop [Fraigniaud2006Reduced]. Bender, Fernández, Ron, Sahai and Vadhan measured what the bound is worth in directed graphs: one pebble suffices when an upper bound on $n$ is known, while without it $\Theta(\log\log n)$ pebbles are necessary and sufficient, the lower bound holding even for randomized robots [Bender2002Pebble]. The top level, a full map, makes static exploration an offline planning task (a known undirected graph is explored by depth-first search in fewer than $2n$ steps); it matters for temporal graphs, where exploration with the whole schedule known in advance was introduced by Michail and Spirakis, who are given the whole temporal graph as input and show that the fastest exploration cannot be approximated within $cn$ for some constant $c > 0$ unless P = NP (Theorem 1) [Michail2016Temporal], and studied by Erlebach, Hoffmann and Kammer [Erlebach2021Temporal].

axes.name: Markers

values.label: one pebble (a movable marker)
values.definition: The agent carries one pebble that it can drop at its current node and later pick up; it sees whether a pebble is at its node.

values.label: several pebbles; their number is a resource
values.definition: The agent carries $p$ pebbles (identical or distinguishable, as stated); $p$ is a resource reported with the memory.

axes.origin: Pebbles come from the tradition of automata in mazes. After Budach proved that no finite automaton explores every finite maze [Budach1978Labyrinths], Blum and Kozen showed that two pebbles suffice for a finite automaton in a maze, against Shah's conjecture that five were needed, and left open whether one pebble suffices [Blum1978Compass]; Hoffmann showed that it does not (as cited by [Disser2019Pebbles]). Cohen, Fraigniaud, Ilcinkas, Korman and Peleg describe this "Rabin's pebble model" as the ability of the robot to label nodes dynamically, at most one unit of label per pebble [Cohen2008Label]. Bender et al. carried the question to directed graphs and agents with unbounded memory, titling their paper "The power of a pebble": one pebble and a bound on $n$ already give polynomial-time mapping [Bender2002Pebble]. In anonymous graphs a marker is what makes stopping possible at all, and by convention a robot asked to stop is given a pebble [Fraigniaud2006Reduced]. The number of pebbles became a resource of its own when Disser, Hackfeld and Klimm showed that $\Theta(\log\log n)$ pebbles are necessary and sufficient for a constant-memory agent on undirected graphs, and that an agent with $O((\log n)^{1-\varepsilon})$ bits already needs $\Omega(\log\log n)$ of them [Disser2019Pebbles]; this is why one pebble and several pebbles are separate levels.

axes.name: Preprocessing

values.label: ports and nodes as given by an adversary
values.definition: Port numbers (and any node labels) are chosen by an adversary.

values.label: port numbers chosen by the designer
values.description: The designer fixes the local port numbering of the graph before the agent starts; used for periodic exploration with tiny memory.
values.definition: Before the agent starts, the designer may choose the port numbering $\mathrm{port}_v:\{\text{edges at }v\}\to\{1,\dots,\deg(v)\}$ at every node. Ilcinkas calls a designer's port numbering a *local orientation* [Ilcinkas2008Ports].

values.label: short node labels chosen by the designer
values.definition: Before the agent starts, the designer may write a label of $b$ bits (a constant) at every node, which the agent reads on arrival.

axes.origin: This axis asks what a designer who prepares the graph before the agent arrives can do for it, a question that grew out of the impossibility results of Budach and Rollik for finite automata [Budach1978Labyrinths] [Rollik1980Planar]. Cohen, Fraigniaud, Ilcinkas, Korman and Peleg let the designer write short labels on the nodes and showed that three label values let a constant-memory robot explore every graph and stop; by Rollik's result two values are the minimum one could hope for [Cohen2008Label]. They place the model next to pebbles: it "can be considered stronger than Rabin's pebble model since labels are given in a preprocessing stage, but it can also be considered weaker since, once assigned to nodes, the labels cannot be modified", and they cite it as part of a line of work on short information supplied in advance, including the oracle-size measure of Fraigniaud, Ilcinkas and Pelc [Cohen2008Label] [Fraigniaud2006Oracle]. Choosing the port numbers is preprocessing that writes nothing on the nodes: Ilcinkas starts from Budach's result that no finite automaton explores all graphs when an adversary sets the local orientation, and asks for the shortest exploration period when the designer sets it, improving the period $10n$ of Dobrev et al. to $4n$ [Ilcinkas2008Ports]. The two forms of preprocessing are kept on the same level because neither is known to simulate the other.

axes.name: Termination requirement

values.label: explore, then stop at the start node
values.definition: The agent visits every node and then halts at its start node $s$.

values.label: explore, then stop anywhere
values.definition: The agent visits every node and then halts, at any node. Also called *terminating exploration*.

values.label: visit every node; never required to stop (perpetual)
values.definition: Every node is visited at least once (and, for periodic exploration, infinitely often); the agent never needs to halt.

axes.origin: The three termination requirements were separated in the memory-bounded exploration literature of the early 2000s. Fraigniaud, Ilcinkas, Peer, Pelc and Peleg list them explicitly, exploration with return, exploration with stop and perpetual exploration, and recall that Diks, Fraigniaud, Kranakis and Pelc showed for trees that exploration with stop needs $\Omega(\log\log\log n)$ bits of memory [Fraigniaud2005Automaton] [Diks2004Tree]; the same paper shows that exploration with return needs $\Omega(\log n)$ bits [Diks2004Tree] (as summarised in [Disser2019Pebbles] and [Czyzowicz2012Periodic]), while perpetual exploration of bounded-degree trees is possible with $O(1)$ bits [Fraigniaud2006Reduced]. In arbitrary anonymous graphs the requirement also decides feasibility: a robot cannot recognise that it has closed a cycle, so without a marker or a bound on $n$ it can explore perpetually but never stop [Fraigniaud2006Reduced]. The axis orders the requirements from the hardest (return) to the weakest (perpetual); periodic exploration, which asks every node to be visited infinitely often within a bounded period, is a perpetual task measured by its period [Ilcinkas2008Ports].

variants.title: Arbitrary graphs, perpetual exploration
variants.summary: The classical memory question: how many bits must a finite-state agent have to visit every node of every graph of diameter $D$ and degree $\Delta$?

preconditions: deterministic agent, no knowledge of the graph
degree $\Delta \ge 3$; the traps are planar
Theorem 4 and Corollary 5: for every $K$-state agent there is a planar trap of degree $\Delta$ and diameter $O(\log K/\log\Delta)$
lower_bounds.note: Corollary 3 gives $\lceil\log n\rceil$ bits directly: for every $K$-state agent there is a planar trap with at most $K+1$ nodes (Theorem 2; with loops and multiple edges, or $K+\Delta+2$ nodes for simple graphs). Earlier: no finite automaton explores all mazes [Budach1978Labyrinths]; no finite team of automata explores all cubic planar graphs [Rollik1980Planar].

results.note: Introductory and current best (Increasing-DFS, Theorem 6 and Corollary 7): depth-first searches of depth $1, 2, 3, \dots$; no knowledge of $D$ or $\Delta$ is needed. The bound is the memory used until exploration is complete; by Theorem 8 any agent that explores all graphs uses unboundedly many states over time.

time.note: The paper does not study time ("time is not an issue in our approach").

memory.note: $\Theta(D\log\Delta)$ bits in the worst case over graphs of diameter $D$ and degree $\Delta$.

open: What is the time of memory-optimal perpetual exploration, and is there a trade-off between memory and time?
variants.notes: In [Fraigniaud2005Automaton] exploring means traversing every edge, not only visiting every node. The model goes back to maze search: Shannon's maze-solving mouse, Budach's theorem that no finite automaton explores all mazes [Budach1978Labyrinths], Blum and Kozen [Blum1978Compass], and Rollik's result that no finite team of automata explores all cubic planar graphs [Rollik1980Planar]. Blum and Kozen proved that a finite automaton with two pebbles, or two automata together, search every maze, and that no three finite automata together can search all finite planar cubic graphs (Theorem 6.1; also one automaton, Theorem 4.1, and two, Theorem 4.6), so mazes, which come with a compass, are strictly easier than graphs; whether any finite team suffices for planar cubic graphs was left open [Blum1978Compass]. Their automata need not halt. This confirms the account of [Fraigniaud2005Automaton]; the reading in [Cohen2008Label] that one agent with three pebbles cannot explore all graphs is not a result of [Blum1978Compass]. Fraigniaud, Ilcinkas and Pelc showed that a polynomial increase in the number of states strictly enlarges the class of explorable regular graphs (DAM 2008, not in the bibliography yet). Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Exploration with stop, nothing known
variants.summary: Without a bound on $n$ and without a way to mark a node, an agent can never be sure it has seen everything.

lower_bounds.bottleneck: no way to recognise the start
preconditions: deterministic agent, no upper bound on $n$, no marking of nodes
unbounded memory does not help
even cycles cannot be explored with stop without a way to mark a node [Fraigniaud2006Reduced]

lower_bounds.bottleneck: no way to recognise the start
preconditions: same conditions as for time

time.note: Feasible with one unmovable token at the start node [Dieudonne2012Tokens].

variants.notes: The impossibility is why every stopping variant below adds either knowledge (a bound on $n$) or a way to mark a node (a pebble or a token). Dieudonné and Pelc also study Byzantine tokens: identical unmovable tokens, some of which may be faulty; exploration is feasible in polynomial cost if a bound on the number of tokens is known and at least one is fault-free [Dieudonne2012Tokens].

variants.title: Exploration with stop when $n$ is known
variants.summary: Reingold's log-space universal exploration sequences give an $O(\log n)$-bit agent that explores and stops in polynomial time.

preconditions: for every constant $\varepsilon>0$
the agent may depend on $n$: it must explore all graphs with at most $n$ nodes
no pebbles; deterministic
lower_bounds.note: Corollary 25 of [Disser2019Pebbles]: with $O((\log n)^{1-\varepsilon})$ bits an agent needs $\Omega(\log\log n)$ pebbles.

results.note: Introductory and current best. A log-space constructible universal exploration sequence [Koucky2002Backtracking] guides a walk through all nodes; the consequence for agents is stated by [Disser2019Pebbles].

time.note: Polynomial; the exponent is not tracked and no non-trivial lower bound is recorded.

memory.note: $O(\log n)$ versus $\omega((\log n)^{1-\varepsilon})$: a $(\log n)^{\varepsilon}$ factor.

open: Is $\Omega(\log n)$ bits necessary when $n$ is known? The trap arguments [Fraigniaud2005Automaton] are stated for agents that know nothing.
variants.notes: Whether the same agent can also return to $s$ (by reversing the sequence) is plausible but not checked against a source.

variants.title: Randomized exploration when $n$ is known
variants.summary: A random walk covers any graph in expected $2m(n-1)$ steps; with a step counter and a bound on $n$ it stops after exploring with good probability.

assumes: stops correctly with constant probability (Monte Carlo)
results.note: Expected cover time at most $2m(n-1)$ from any start (Theorem 4). Running the walk for a multiple of that many steps with an $O(\log n)$-bit counter gives the Monte Carlo agent.

time.note: No lower bound recorded for randomized agents.

memory.note: No lower bound recorded for randomized agents.

open: What is the memory needed by a randomized agent that must stop correctly with high probability, as a function of $n$?
variants.notes: The same paper proves by the probabilistic method that universal traversal sequences of length $O(n^3\log n)$ exist for connected $\Delta$-regular graphs, the constant depending on $\Delta$ (the proof uses length $2\Delta n(n-1)(\Delta n+2)\lceil\log n\rceil$) [Aleliunas1979Random]. For directed graphs the cover time can be exponential, while Eulerian digraphs behave like undirected graphs [Aleliunas1979Random]; Reingold later constructed universal exploration sequences in log space [Reingold2008Undirected].

variants.title: Exploration with stop and one pebble
variants.summary: One pebble makes stopping possible; the agent then needs $\Omega(\log n)$ bits.

preconditions: deterministic agent with one pebble that starts on the agent's start node
no knowledge of $n$
the traps are edge-coloured regular graphs of size $O(K^3)$ for a $K$-state agent (Theorem 5 of [Fraigniaud2006Reduced])

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 3, DFS-with-stop): the pebble marks the start; depth-first phases of depth $1, 2, \dots$ detect new nodes, and the agent stops after phase $D+1$. No knowledge of $D$ or $\Delta$. Time is not analysed.

memory.note: $O(D\log\Delta)$ versus $\Omega(\log n)$: polynomial when $D$ is large.

open: Is $\Omega(D\log\Delta)$ memory needed for exploration with stop by an agent with one pebble [Fraigniaud2005Space]?
variants.notes: The same authors show that $k$ non-cooperative agents need $\Omega(\log(n/k))$ bits for perpetual exploration, with traps of size $O(kK)$ [Fraigniaud2006Reduced]. That chapter is inconsistent on tightness: a remark calls the $\Omega(\log n)$ bound tight, citing the SIROCCO paper, while its conclusion says a tight bound for terminating exploration is open. Checked against the full texts.

variants.title: Exploration with return and pebbles
variants.summary: $\Theta(\log\log n)$ pebbles are necessary and sufficient for a constant-memory agent, which then explores in polynomial time and returns to the start without knowing $n$.

preconditions: for any agent with $O((\log n)^{1-\varepsilon})$ bits
holds for every termination requirement
deterministic

results.note: Introductory and current best (SODA 2016 for bounded degree, JACM 2019 in general). Since $p+1$ agents can simulate one agent with $p$ pebbles, the same bounds hold for teams: $\Theta(\log\log n)$ constant-memory agents.

time.note: Polynomial; the exponent is not tracked.

open: How much memory is needed to encode the agent's transition function? The naive table needs $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ bits (Remark 1 of [Disser2019Pebbles]).
variants.notes: The trade-off reads: $\Omega(\log n)$ bits make pebbles unnecessary; $O((\log n)^{1-\varepsilon})$ bits force $\Omega(\log\log n)$ pebbles; $\Omega(\log\log n)$ pebbles make $O(1)$ bits enough. The traps of [Disser2019Pebbles] have $O(K^{2^{5k}})$ nodes for $k$ agents with $K$ states, improving Rollik's tower-type bound [Rollik1980Planar].

variants.title: Memoryless automaton with pebbles
variants.summary: A deterministic memoryless automaton (one state) explores every connected graph with 2 pebbles, and 2 is the minimum.
variants.statement: The agent is a deterministic finite automaton with a single state: its decision depends only on what it observes at the current node (entry port, degree, pebbles present), not on a state. It carries $p$ pebbles labelled $1,\dots,p$, which it can drop and pick up. Exploration is complete when every edge has been traversed at least once.

preconditions: one pebble is insufficient in general, even if $n$ is known
a memoryless automaton without pebbles cannot explore all graphs

results.note: Introductory and current best. If $n$ is known and the automaton starts at a node with a pebble, one pebble suffices.

memory.note: Two pebbles are necessary and sufficient.

variants.notes: Results from the paper's abstract, supplied by the catalogue owner (a co-author).

variants.title: Trees, perpetual exploration
variants.summary: On trees, perpetual exploration needs exactly $\Theta(\log\Delta)$ bits: enough to remember a port.

preconditions: trees of maximum degree $\Delta$
deterministic

results.note: Introductory and current best. Equivalently, the sequence $1^n$ is a universal exploration sequence for trees [Koucky2002Backtracking]: leave by the port after the entry port.

time.note: Time not stated in the sources read.

variants.title: Trees, exploration with stop
variants.summary: Stopping on a tree without knowing $n$ needs more than constant memory, but how much more is open: $\Omega(\log\log\log n)$ against $O(\log n)$.

preconditions: bounded-degree trees built from paths
$n$ unknown
deterministic

results.note: Via exploration with return, which implies stop.

open: Can exploration with stop on trees use asymptotically less memory than exploration with return? (Open problem of [Diks2004Tree].) Equivalently: close $\Omega(\log\log\log n)$ versus $O(\log n)$.
variants.notes: If an upper bound $N$ on $n$ is known, $O(\log N)$ bits suffice; if a bound $m$ on the number of nodes of some degree is known, $O(\log\Delta+\log m)$ bits [Diks2004Tree]. "The additional memory is essentially needed to decide when to stop."

variants.title: Trees, exploration with return
variants.summary: Returning to the start on a tree takes $\Theta(\log n)$ bits.

preconditions: every $n$-node tree
deterministic
holds even if the agent knows the tree up to its start node, so knowing $n$ does not help

results.note: Also works when ports are only circularly ordered.

time.note: Time not stated in the abstracts read.

variants.notes: [Diks2004Tree] asked for the exact memory of exploration with return; [Ambuhl2011Tree] answered it.

variants.title: Node labels chosen by the designer
variants.summary: With three-valued labels on the nodes, an agent with fewer than 25 states explores every graph and stops after at most $20m$ edge traversals.

assumes: labels of 2 bits (3 values), computed in linear time
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 2.1): fewer than 25 states, at most $20m$ edge traversals, stops at a node chosen by the designer. Labelling while exploring gives $O(Dm)$.
Theorem 3.1.

time.note: Only the trivial $\Omega(n)$ is known against $O(m)$.

variants.notes: The agent is a Mealy automaton: its output port depends on the input port. Agents with a single state cannot explore all graphs with such labels (Theorems 4.2 and 4.5 of [Cohen2008Label]). Recent work changes the model: zero-memory agents that do not see the entry port but may colour nodes (SIROCCO 2023, OPODIS 2025); these are not catalogued yet. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: Port numbers chosen by the designer (periodic exploration)
variants.summary: If the designer may set the port numbers, a constant-memory agent visits every node periodically with period between $2n-2$ and $3.5n-2$.

preconditions: any agent, whatever its memory: on a tree every edge is traversed in both directions
folklore, stated in [Czyzowicz2012Periodic] and [Gasieniec2008Periodic]
for oblivious agents the bound is $2.8n - O(1)$: for $n = 5k + l$ with $l < 5$ some $n$-node graph has no witness cycle shorter than $14k + 2l$ (Theorem 13 of [Czyzowicz2012Periodic])

results.note: Theorem 1; the abstract rounds the period to $4n$.
Period less than $3.75n-2$ (Theorem 2), with port numbers set along a spanning tree; this disproved Ilcinkas's conjecture that $4n - O(1)$ is optimal for any memory [Ilcinkas2008Ports].
For oblivious agents the same paper gives $(4+\tfrac13)n-4$; the best oblivious period is $4n-2$ [Kosowski2012Decomposition].

assumes: oblivious agent following the right-hand rule: it leaves by port $(i \bmod \deg(v)) + 1$ after entering by port $i$
results.note: Theorem 3; the labelling is computed in polynomial time (Theorem 4). It is the best possible for labellings in which the edges traversed twice form a connected spanning subgraph: $K_{2,l}$ needs $4n-8$ under that restriction (Theorem 5).

time.note: $\Theta(n)$; the constant is open: $2n-2$ versus $3.5n-2$ (constant memory), $2.8n - O(1)$ versus $4n-2$ (oblivious).

open: Close the constant gaps: $2n-2$ versus $3.5n-2$ for constant memory, $2.8n - O(1)$ versus $4n-2$ for oblivious agents [Czyzowicz2012Periodic] [Kosowski2012Decomposition].
Trade-offs between period and memory: the only lower bound for agents with memory does not depend on memory.
variants.notes: Without the designer's help, periodic exploration by a finite automaton is impossible (Budach, as cited by [Czyzowicz2012Periodic]). These papers began with Dobrev, Jansson, Sadakane and Sung (SIROCCO 2005; period $10n$, as cited by [Czyzowicz2012Periodic]). Computing the shortest witness cycle for an oblivious agent is NP-hard. The period is defined differently: Ilcinkas counts returns to a node in the same state through the same port, Czyzowicz et al. returns to a node through the same port. For oblivious agents the right-hand rule is no restriction: the shortest period over all labellings is the same for every oblivious strategy, as Kosowski and Navarra note citing [Czyzowicz2012Periodic] [Kosowski2012Decomposition].

variants.title: Directed graphs, one pebble
variants.summary: An agent that cannot walk back along an arc needs $\Omega(n\log\Delta_{out})$ bits, even with up to $n$ pebbles; with one pebble, $O(n\Delta_{out}\log n)$ bits suffice, in exponential time.

preconditions: strongly connected digraphs, maximum out-degree $\Delta_{out}$; the agent is a deterministic finite automaton

a combination lock (Definition 1): nodes $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$, all of out-degree $\Delta_{out}$; each $u_i$ with $i < n-1$ has one arc to $u_{i+1}$ and its other arcs to $u_0$, and every arc of $u_{n-1}$ leads to $u_0$
proved for perpetual exploration (Theorem 1), so it holds for exploration with stop
holds even with up to $n$ pebbles when $\Delta_{out} > 2$, and with up to $n/2$ pebbles when $\Delta_{out} = 2$

results.note: Introductory and current best (Algorithm Test-all-maps, Theorem 2). The agent needs no knowledge of $n$: it tries $n = 1, 2, \dots$ and every map of order $n$ in turn, checking each with its pebble, so the time is exponential in the worst case. With whiteboards instead of a pebble, constant agent memory and $O(\log\Delta_{out})$ bits per node suffice.

time.note: The one-pebble algorithm takes exponential time; there is no lower bound on time beyond the trivial one.

open: Close $\Omega(n\log\Delta_{out})$ versus $O(n\Delta_{out}\log n)$ bits for exploring digraphs with one pebble.

Determine the trade-off between time and memory: polynomial-time exploration with stop is known only with $O(n^2\Delta_{out}\log n)$ bits and $O(\log\log n)$ pebbles, far from the $\Omega(n\log\Delta_{out})$ lower bound (Section 5 of [Fraigniaud2004Digraphs]).
variants.notes: Here $\Delta_{out}$ is the maximum out-degree ($d$ in [Fraigniaud2004Digraphs]). With $O(\log\log n)$ pebbles, Algorithm Compacted-Explore-and-Map, a variant of the algorithm of [Bender2002Pebble], explores with stop in polynomial time using $O(n^2\Delta_{out}\log n)$ bits (Theorem 3), and $\Omega(\log\log n)$ pebbles are necessary for polynomial time when no bound on $n$ is known [Bender2002Pebble]. Without any memory an agent cannot explore with stop even with whiteboards (Theorem 4). Bender and Slonim showed that two cooperating agents learn any unlabelled digraph in expected polynomial time [Bender1994Team]. Checked against the full text of [Fraigniaud2004Digraphs] (model, Theorems 1 to 4 and the conclusion).

variants.title: Directed graphs, one pebble, bound on $n$ known
variants.summary: With a bound $N \ge n$, one pebble lets an agent map any strongly connected digraph in polynomial time.

assumes: all out-degrees padded to $\Delta_{out}$ with self-loops; $\Delta_{out}$ known
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 3.1; $N$ is the paper's $\hat n$, $\Delta_{out}$ its $d$). Without a bound on $n$, for every constant $c>0$, $c\log\log n$ pebbles give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm (Theorem 4.1), and $\Omega(\log\log n)$ pebbles are necessary for any algorithm, even randomized, that learns every graph in expected polynomial time with probability greater than $1/2$ (Theorem 4.2).

time.note: No lower bound beyond the trivial $\Omega(m)$.

memory.note: Memory is not bounded in these papers.

open: Improve the $O(N^2 n^6 \Delta_{out}^2)$ running time (Section 5 of [Bender2002Pebble]).
variants.notes: Checked against the full text of [Bender2002Pebble]. The agent must output a graph isomorphic to $G$; it sees out-ports numbered $1,\dots,\Delta_{out}$ but not in-degrees, and cannot retrace an arc to fetch its pebble. Bender and Slonim had shown that a constant number of pebbles does not suffice for polynomial time when no bound on $n$ is known (as cited in [Bender2002Pebble]). With labelled nodes a greedy search takes $O(nm)$ moves.

variants.title: Directed graphs with labelled nodes
variants.summary: An agent that recognises nodes but cannot backtrack must traverse every arc; the cost depends on the deficiency $\phi$ of the digraph.

preconditions: deficiency $\phi$: the number of arcs to add to make the digraph Eulerian
deterministic strategies; the argument does not apply to randomized ones
due to Koutsoupias: Corollary 3 of [Deng1999Exploring] gives at least $\phi^2/4$ times the number of arcs
lower_bounds.note: Deng and Papadimitriou's own bound (Theorem 1) is about $\phi^2 m/(2\log\phi)$; against randomized strategies they show a ratio of $\Omega(\phi/\log\phi)$ to the optimal tour (Corollary 2).

results.note: Theorem 3: no arc is traversed more than $2^{O(\phi\log\phi)}$ times, without knowing $\phi$. Eulerian digraphs ($\phi=0$): ratio 2 to the optimal tour, which is optimal; deficiency one: no arc traversed more than four times (Theorem 2).
First subexponential algorithm; the authors also show that their algorithm needs $\phi^{\Omega(\log\phi)}m$ on some graphs, and that Greedy, Depth-First and Breadth-First need $2^{\Omega(\phi)}m$.
First algorithm polynomial in $\phi$; the paper itself was not read, the bound is from the authors' abstract.

memory.note: Memory is not bounded in these papers.

open: Close $\Omega(\phi^2m)$ versus $O(\phi^8m)$ for online exploration of digraphs with deficiency $\phi$.
variants.notes: This is the online-algorithms tradition: nodes are recognisable and the agent builds a map; cost is compared with the optimal tour (the Chinese postman tour), and Deng and Papadimitriou note that measured in absolute terms $\Theta(nm)$ is trivially tight. Checked against the full texts of [Deng1999Exploring] and [Albers2000Exploring]; the bound of [Fleischer2005Exploring] is still from the authors' abstract. The deficiency was introduced by Kutten [Kutten1988Stepwise]. For the related objective of visiting every node (not every arc), Foerster and Wattenhofer show a competitive ratio linear in $n$, with deterministic and randomized upper and lower bounds tight up to small constants (abstract read) [Foerster2016Lower].

variants.title: Dynamic rings
variants.summary: On a $T$-interval-connected ring whose edges may be missing for up to $\delta$ steps, the worst-case exploration time is known exactly up to additive terms.

preconditions: underlying graph a ring
the agent does not know the dynamics
$T$-interval connectivity; $\delta$ = longest absence of an edge

results.note: Introductory and current best. If the agent knows the dynamics, the worst case is $2n-T-\Theta(1)$.

variants.notes: Multi-agent exploration of dynamic rings and graphs, where the measure is how many agents are needed (Di Luna, Dobrev, Flocchini and Santoro; Gotoh, Flocchini, Masuzawa and Santoro), is not catalogued yet.

variants.title: Temporal graphs, schedule known
variants.summary: If the whole schedule of an always-connected temporal graph is known, $\Theta(n^2)$ steps are necessary and sufficient in the worst case.

preconditions: an explicit family of always-connected temporal graphs
holds for centralised, offline exploration
underlying graph (the union of all snapshots) of maximum degree at most $\Delta$, for $\Delta_0 \le \Delta \le n-1$ with an absolute constant $\Delta_0$
every snapshot is a spanning tree in which only one node has degree above three; deterministic construction, polynomial in $n$
holds from every start node; also a lower bound when only the degree of each snapshot is at most $\Delta$
lower_bounds.note: Theorem 1.1 (arXiv v1). In each phase of $\Theta(\Delta n)$ steps, a cycle whose missing edge advances by one position per step lets the agent enter fewer than half of $\Theta(\Delta)$ branches; between phases the nodes not yet visited are reassigned among the branches along walks on an expander, which allows $\Theta(1+\log(n/\Delta))$ phases. One construction thus combines the $\Omega(\Delta n)$ of chained rotating stars [Erlebach2021Temporal] and the $\Omega(n\log n)$ known for planar underlying graphs of maximum degree 4, both as reported by [Carnevale2026Hiding]; for constant $\Delta$ it adds nothing to $\Omega(n\log n)$. Preprint.

results.note: The $n^2$ upper bound is attributed by the authors to Michail and Spirakis. They also give $O(n^{1.5}\mathrm{tw}^{1.5}\log n)$ for treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, $O(n^{1.8}\log n)$ for planar and $2n-2$ for cycles, and show inapproximability within $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$.

Parameterized by $\sigma$, the number of classes of the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman colouring of the temporal graph (their $q$), $1 \le \sigma \le n$; vertex-transitive and distance-regular underlying graphs have $\sigma = 1$. The walk is computed deterministically in polynomial time, for a long enough lifetime (Theorem 1.1). Some instances need $\Omega(n\log n)$ steps for constant $\sigma$ and $\Omega(\sigma n)$ for every $\sigma$ (Theorem 1.3), so the bound is tight up to polylogarithmic factors. It improves an earlier bound in the number of automorphism orbits (at least $\sigma$), which needed superpolynomial computation, as reported by [Kammer2026Weisfeiler].

assumes: at most $\mu \ge 2$ edges of the underlying graph missing in each snapshot
results.note: Corollary 1.3 (arXiv v1; their $k$ is $\mu$ here), for always-connected temporal graphs with enough snapshots, from any start node. It suffices that at most $\mu$ edges of one fixed spanning tree of the underlying graph are missing in each snapshot (Theorem 1.1). The schedule is computed by a Las Vegas algorithm in expected polynomial time, and deterministically in polynomial time when $\mu$ is constant (Theorem 1.2). It improves the $O(\mu n\log n)$ of Erlebach and Spooner and is within a factor $\mu$ of their $\Omega(n\log\mu)$ lower bound, both as reported by [Lahtin2026Exploration]; for constant $\mu$ exploration takes $\Theta(n)$ steps.

Theorem 2 of the full version (arXiv v2). The underlying graph is divided into parts with few boundary nodes; each part is explored by a team of agents (Theorem 1, on always $S$-connected temporal graphs, in which every snapshot joins every node to some node of a fixed set $S$), and the team schedule is turned into one for a single agent. For small $\mathrm{tw}$ it is below the $O(n^{3/2}\sqrt{\mathrm{tw}}\log n)$ of Bastide, Groenland, Michel and Rambaud, as reported by [Adamson2026Exploration]. [Carnevale2026Hiding] cites $\mathrm{tw}^{11/2}$ for the brief announcement, which was not read.

open: Tight bounds when the underlying graph is a grid, has bounded degree or is planar [Erlebach2021Temporal].

For underlying maximum degree $\Delta$, close the gap between $\Omega(\Delta n(1+\log(n/\Delta)))$ [Carnevale2026Hiding] and $O(\min\{n^2, n^{3/2}\sqrt{\Delta}\log n\})$ (the latter as reported by [Carnevale2026Hiding]); for constant $\Delta$ the bounds are $\Omega(n\log n)$ and $O(n^{3/2}\log n)$.
When at most $\mu$ edges are missing in each snapshot, remove the factor $\mu$ between $O(\mu n\log\mu)$ [Lahtin2026Exploration] and $\Omega(n\log\mu)$ (as reported by [Lahtin2026Exploration]).
variants.notes: This is a centralised planning problem rather than a distributed one, but it gives the baseline for what any agent could do in a temporal graph.

variants.title: $T$-interval-connected graphs, labelled nodes
variants.summary: On a $T$-interval-connected graph whose nodes carry identifiers, a deterministic agent can explore every graph with $m$ edges only if $T = \Omega(m)$; with a slightly larger window it explores and stops within $\Theta(n^3)$ moves in the worst case, and within $\Theta(n^2)$ if it also sees its neighbours' identifiers.
variants.statement: The graph is a dynamic graph $(G_t)_{t \ge 0}$ on a fixed node set; its underlying graph (all edges that ever appear) is simple and connected, with $n$ nodes and $m \ge n$ edges. It is $T$-interval connected: for every $t$, the edges present in all of the rounds $t, \dots, t+T-1$ form a connected spanning subgraph. Every node carries a distinct identifier. In round $t$ the agent at node $v$ sees the identifier of $v$, $\deg(v)$ in the underlying graph, which ports of $v$ have their edge present in $G_t$, and the port by which it entered; it then crosses one present edge or stops (staying put only uses up the window). The agent is deterministic and knows neither $T$, $n$ nor $m$; it must visit every node and stop. Two quantities are asked for: the smallest window $T$, as a function of $n$ and $m$, for which some algorithm explores every $T$-interval-connected graph, and the number of moves it then needs. With **1-hop view** (the model KT$_1$ of [Sudo2026Tight]; the setting above is their KT$_0$) the agent also sees the identifiers of its neighbours in $G_t$ and the ports that lead to them.

preconditions: deterministic agent that sees only its own node (KT$_0$); $n$ large enough and $n \le m \le \binom n2$
holds for every window $T$: a spanning path is present in every round ($\infty$-interval connected)

the underlying graph is a path $v_1, \dots, v_n$, plus $\min(m-n+1, |V_L|\,|V_R|)$ trap edges between $V_L$ (the first third of the path) and $V_R$ (its last third without $v_n$), plus edges that are never present while the agent is at one of their ends; the agent starts at $v_1$

the adversary removes the trap edges at every node of $V_L$ the agent visits, and, since the agent learns where a port leads only by crossing its edge, sends every unused port of a node of $V_R$ along an unused trap edge
lower_bounds.note: Theorem 4: each trap edge costs a walk of $\Omega(n)$ moves back to $V_R$ before $v_n$ is reached.

preconditions: window $T \le \kappa m$ for a small enough constant $\kappa > 0$ (Theorem 3): for every $n$ large enough and every $m$ with $n \le m \le \binom n2$, some $T$-interval-connected graph with $n$ nodes and $m$ edges has a node that the agent never visits
deterministic agent; holds with 1-hop view and even for perpetual exploration

for $m \ge 2n$: two copies of $K_g$ minus one edge, $g = \lfloor\sqrt{m/8}\rfloor$, joined through three nodes and one edge, with a path attached; an agent that enters a copy can be kept inside it for $\Omega(g^2)$ rounds without disconnecting any window (Lemma 9, which holds even if the agent knows the underlying graph with its ports)
for $n \le m < 2n$: a ring whose two edges at one node are removed alternately, which keeps the graph $(n-3)$-interval connected
lower_bounds.note: With the algorithms below, the smallest window is $\Theta(m)$ when $m = n^{1+\Omega(1)}$, and $\Theta(n^2)$ as a function of $n$ alone (Corollary 2), with or without 1-hop view.

preconditions: with 1-hop view (KT$_1$); deterministic agent
holds for every window $T$ ($\infty$-interval connected)
a path of $n-g$ nodes attached to $K_g$ minus one edge, $g = \lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor$; the agent starts inside the $K_g$ part and is kept there for $\Omega(g^2)$ rounds (Lemma 9)
lower_bounds.note: Theorem 5. It bounds the time of the 1-hop-view algorithm below; the first bound is the one for this setting.

assumes: window $T \ge \kappa(\zeta m + n\log^2 n)$ for a large enough constant $\kappa$, where $\zeta = \zeta(n,m) = \frac{\ln n}{1 + \ln m - \ln n}$
unbounded memory: the agent keeps a map of the nodes and edges it has seen
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 1, algorithm GreedyExp$_0$; $\zeta$ is their $\epsilon(n,m)$). The agent walks, along edges it has never seen missing, to the nearest visited node that has an unused port whose edge was present at every visit, and crosses that edge. Every $\kappa(\zeta m' + n'\log^2 n')$ moves, with $n'$ and $m'$ computed from the nodes and ports seen so far, it forgets which edges it saw missing, so that each such period has a spanning tree present throughout. A period that does not end the exploration contains at least $\kappa(\zeta m' + n'\log^2 n')/(2n')$ crossings of unused edges into visited nodes (Lemma 8), and there are at most $m-n+1$ such crossings (Corollary 4).

assumes: window $T \ge \kappa(\zeta m + n\log^2 n)$ for a large enough constant $\kappa$; $T$, $n$ and $m$ unknown
results.note: Theorem 2, algorithm GreedyExp$_1$: walk to the nearest node seen but not visited, in the map of edges never seen missing. Exploration ends within the window itself, so one spanning tree is present throughout. The distance to the nearest unvisited node grows by at most $2n\log n$ in total when new nodes are visited (Lemma 4) and by $O(\zeta m + n\log^2 n)$ when edges are seen missing, through the bound $|E| \le \tfrac12|V|^{1+1/j} + \tfrac12|V|$ for graphs of girth at least $2j+1$ (Lemmas 5 and 6).

time.note: $O((m-n+1)\,n + n\log^2 n)$ against $\Omega((m-n+1)\,n)$: tight when $m - n + 1 = \Omega(\log^2 n)$, and $\Theta(n^3)$ as a function of $n$ alone. With 1-hop view, $O(\zeta m + n\log^2 n)$ against $\Omega(m)$: at most a $\log^2 n$ factor, and $\Theta(n^2)$ in $n$ alone. The window needed is between $\Omega(m)$ and $O(\zeta m + n\log^2 n)$ for both views.

memory.note: Memory is not bounded: the agent keeps a map.

open: Close the gap on the window, $\Omega(m)$ against $O(\zeta m + n\log^2 n)$; it is at most a $\log^2 n$ factor and remains when $m = n^{1+o(1)}$ [Sudo2026Tight].
How much smaller can the window be, and how much faster the exploration, for a randomized agent [Sudo2026Tight]?
Close the polylogarithmic gap on the time with 1-hop view, $\Omega(m)$ against $O(\zeta m + n\log^2 n)$, and determine exactly what the 1-hop view buys [Sudo2026Tight].
variants.notes: Sudo, Kitamura, Shibata, Nakamura, Tixeuil, Masuzawa and Wada study a single deterministic agent on $T$-interval-connected graphs of arbitrary topology [Sudo2026Tight]. They assume $m \ge n$, since with $m = n-1$ every edge is always present and the graph is static. Their lower bounds on time hold even if one spanning tree is present forever: the cost comes from edges that are absent while the agent stands at one of their ends, not from disconnection. On rings the window has to be large as well (the case $m < 2n$ of Theorem 3); this is why the online exploration of $T$-interval-connected rings [Ilcinkas2018Ring] also assumes that every edge appears at least once in every $\delta$ consecutive rounds, as Sudo et al. recall. Both algorithms rely on the identifiers: the agent recognises the nodes it has visited and keeps a map of the edges it has seen. Checked against the full text (arXiv v1, 2026), a preprint.

further.note: Bhagat and Pelc: a deterministic finite automaton in the infinite anonymous oriented grid $\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z$ (ports N, E, S, W at every node) must visit every node of a given wedge, the grid nodes between two rays from a common origin, whose directions are built into the automaton. Each ray is a wall (the edges across it are blocked) or free, and the agent starts at a node of the wedge chosen by an adversary (at the origin for a wedge with two free rays). The minimum number of pebbles is 0, 1 and 2 for wedges of angle below $\pi$ with two walls, one wall and no wall, and 1, 2 and 3 for angles of at least $\pi$ (Theorems 2.1–2.5 and 3.1–3.5, Corollaries 2.1, 2.2, 3.1 and 3.2); a narrow walled wedge can be disconnected, and then the component of the start node is explored. The impossibilities for wedges with two free rays follow from bounds on teams of two and of three automata in the grid by Emek, Langner, Stolz, Uitto and Wattenhofer and by Brandt, Uitto and Wattenhofer, as cited there. This is perpetual exploration of one given infinite graph, which no setting of this problem covers. Read (arXiv v1, 2023).

Exploration with the schedule known when every edge of the underlying graph is present at least once in every $F$ consecutive steps, no snapshot being required to be connected: one agent explores from any start node within $F(2n-3)$ steps by following a spanning tree of minimum total waiting time (Theorem 3.5, Lemma 3.6), and a star in which all edges but one are present only every $F$-th step needs $F(2n-5)+1$ steps (Theorem 3.10, Corollary 3.11); edges present periodically with period at most $F$ are a special case (Corollary 3.8). Consequences for public-transport timetables (Theorem 4.1), for graphs in which each node opens one incoming edge per step in a fixed cyclic order ($4m$ steps, Theorem 4.2) and for broadcast networks (Corollary 4.4, Theorem 4.6). Preprint; read.

Exploration with the schedule known, for temporal graphs given by a word over the nodes: the word is cut into factors without a repeated symbol, one per step, and an edge of the underlying graph (a pair of symbols that alternate in the word) is present in a step when one of its end nodes occurs in that factor. If every snapshot is connected, one agent explores within $2n\cdot\min_v \deg(v)$ steps, the degree taken in the underlying graph (Theorem 4). If only the underlying graph is connected, with diameter $D$ (their $d$), and the word has length at least $n(2Dn+D)$, it explores within $2Dn$ steps (Theorem 11), and for all $n$ and $D$ some such temporal graph needs $\Omega(Dn)$ steps (Theorem 22). Preprint; read.

Random temporal graphs in which every snapshot is a spanning tree drawn independently from a fixed distribution over a set of trees on the $n$ nodes. With high probability an agent that knows the whole sequence explores within $O(n^{3/2})$ steps (Theorem 1.1), which is tight for the uniform distribution over $\lceil n/3\rceil$ stars (Theorem 5.4), and within $54m$ steps when all trees are spanning trees of one graph with $m$ edges (Theorem 1.2). Trees of maximum degree $\Delta$ can force $\Omega(\sqrt{\Delta}\,n)$ steps (Theorem 5.12, odd $\Delta \ge 5$), and $O(\sqrt{\Delta}\,n)$ is conjectured (Conjecture 1.3). An agent that sees only the current snapshot needs $\Omega(n\log n)$ steps on some such model to succeed with probability $1-n^{-\Omega(1)}$ (Proposition 4.4), and more than $n^2/15$ steps with high probability on $n/2$ uniform stars (Proposition 5.13). Read.

Shortest temporal exploration: in an always-connected temporal graph whose whole schedule is known, the agent minimises the number of edges it traverses rather than its arrival time. With lifetime at least $12n^{3.5}+4n$ some exploration traverses $O(n^{1.5})$ edges (Theorem 12), against the $O(n^2)$ implied by the arrival-time bound; if every snapshot has diameter at most some parameter, fewer edges than that parameter times $n$ suffice within that parameter times $n^2$ steps (Theorem 13); on a temporal ring with lifetime at least $2n-2$, $\lfloor 3(n-1)/2\rfloor$ edges suffice and may be needed, whereas with lifetime exactly $2n-3$ an exploration may need $2n-3$ edges (Lemmas 16 to 18). The authors conjecture that every always-connected temporal graph has an exploration of $\Theta(n^2)$ steps that traverses $\Theta(n)$ edges. Preprint; read.

An agent with binoculars (it sees the graph within a constant distance) can explore an anonymous graph and stop in many graphs that are not trees: a characterisation of the graphs explorable this way by simple connectivity of a clique complex, with a universal algorithm that explores each of them and never stops elsewhere (Theorem 1). Read (arXiv v1).

A different model, a metamorphic robotic system: anonymous oblivious modules on the square grid that slide or rotate while staying connected search an unknown finite grid for a target. Three modules with a common compass are necessary and sufficient from any initial shape (Theorem 1); without a compass, five modules are necessary and sufficient from restricted initial shapes (Theorem 4). Read (arXiv v2).
How much advice an agent needs to explore an anonymous graph in a given time, from an oracle that knows the whole instance or only the map. Abstract read.
Which families of anonymous graphs can be explored deterministically without knowledge: a characterisation, and whether one universal algorithm explores every explorable family. Abstract read.

An agent with $M_a$ bits of memory and $M_w$ bits per node that does not learn its entry port: one bit of agent memory changes what can be explored compared with the rotor-router, a $(0, \log d)$-agent. A brief announcement; introduction read.
A survey of space complexity: $\Theta(\log n)$ bits are necessary and sufficient to explore all $n$-node graphs, and with sublogarithmic memory $\Theta(\log\log n)$ agents are needed. Abstract read.

Distance-constrained exploration: the agent must always know a path of length at most $(1+\alpha)r$ back to its start, with $r$ the eccentricity of the start; the penalty is the number of traversals beyond the edges. Abstract read.

Exploration of the fault-free component when some edges are faulty: a perfectly competitive algorithm for rings, and depth-first search is within $10/9$ of the best overhead on Hamiltonian graphs. Abstract read.

Finding a treasure in the $n$-dimensional infinite grid by finite-state agents that start together: three randomised synchronous agents suffice for every $n$, disproving a conjecture that $n+1$ are needed. Abstract read.
A mobile agent that reads and changes marks on nodes and edges explores a finite undirected graph in $O(n^3)$ time with $O(n^2)$ space. Abstract read.
A further marking algorithm for exploring finite undirected graphs by one agent. Abstract read.
Computing optimal offline exploration paths in grid environments for a robot with limited visibility (AAAI 2012). Abstract read.

A single agent that knows the dynamics explores constantly connected dynamic graphs whose underlying graph is a cactus in $O(n\log n/\log\log n)$ time units, with a near-matching lower bound. Abstract read.
Exploration of carrier-based time-varying networks (carriers on periodic routes) when the agent may wait at stations. Abstract read.
Exploration with return of constantly connected dynamic rings: $3n-4$ time units are necessary and sufficient. Abstract read.
Kernelization of non-strict temporal exploration of a given temporal graph. A preprint; abstract read.
Temporal graph exploration is NP-complete even when the underlying graph has pathwidth 2 and every snapshot is connected. A preprint; abstract read.
Restless temporal exploration (the agent must move at every step) of periodic temporal graphs: polynomial for period 2, hard otherwise. Abstract read.

Three semi-synchronous agents running one finite automaton (distinct initial states, sensing only agents in the same cell) cannot explore the infinite grid, answering a question of Emek et al. Abstract read.

A deterministic finite automaton in a convex open region of the plane: it sees the disc of radius 1 around it, moves less than 1 per step, and must eventually see every point, with movable pebbles to mark places. Convex regions are bounded ones, cups, belts, half-planes and the plane (Theorem 1). Bounded regions need no pebble (Theorem 2), cups and belts exactly two (Corollaries 1, 2), half-planes and the plane exactly three (Theorems 5, 6, Corollary 3; the lower bound uses the grid result of [Brandt2020Tight]); the agent knows the type of region but not the region or its start. Read in full.

Reingold, Trevisan and Vadhan carry the log-space method of [Reingold2008Undirected] over to directed graphs in which every node has the same in-degree and out-degree $D$ (biregular digraphs): a deterministic log-space algorithm finds a path between two given nodes. The algorithm yields a log-space constructible universal traversal sequence, a sequence of port numbers that leads a walk from any start node of any graph in the family through every node, for biregular digraphs whose labelling is consistent (at each node the incoming arcs carry distinct labels); every biregular digraph has such a labelling. They also give a log-space pseudorandom walk for these graphs, and show that extending it to every labelling of biregular digraphs would give RL = L. Read: abstract and introduction of the ECCC report TR05-022 (2005).

Rivest and Schapire learn an unknown finite automaton, a directed graph whose arcs are labelled by actions and whose nodes show outputs, from its input/output behaviour alone, without a reset that returns it to a start state; their motivating example is a robot in an unfamiliar environment. The key tool is a homing sequence, a sequence of actions whose observed outputs determine the state reached. With a teacher who answers wrong conjectures by counterexamples, the algorithm outputs a correct description with any prescribed probability of success, in time polynomial in the size of the automaton, the length of the longest counterexample and the logarithm of the inverse failure probability. For permutation automata they give probabilistic algorithms that need no teacher. [Bender1994Team] introduce a homing sequence for two agents and need no teacher. Read: abstract and first page (scanned journal version).

figure.caption: Exploration of a tree by the rule Choose-Next of [Diks2004Tree]: the agent leaves the start node $s$ by port 1 and, entering a node of degree $d$ by port $i$, leaves by port $(i \bmod d) + 1$. It walks around the tree, each edge once in each direction, and is back at $s$ after $2(n-1)$ moves with every node visited (perpetual exploration repeats this tour). One frame per move.

frames.label: Start: one agent at s; ports 1..d at each node
Entered by port i: leave by port (i mod d) + 1
Final: back at s after 2(n-1) = 12 moves; all 7 nodes visited
